blocks.text: — — — let the violent screech-owl sing from the roofs.
Propertius, book 4, in the Letter of Arethusa to Lycotas:
Or whether the owl moaned, perched on the neighbouring beam.
And the greatest Poet, book 1 of the Georgics:
— — — — from the highest rooftop the owl plies her late songs in vain.
And in the passage cited a little earlier:
And alone on the rooftops the eagle-owl with funereal song.

But examples of this kind also occur everywhere in the Historians. Lampridius, on the [col. 156] death of the emperor Commodus: An eagle-owl was also caught above his bedchamber, both at Rome and at Lavinium. Above the bedchamber, that is, above the roof of the bedchamber. Dio also, in his Commodus: Ὁ βύας ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῦ ἔβυξεν [Ho byas ep᾽ autou ebyxen], the eagle-owl hooted upon it (that is, upon the roof of the Capitol). For so some read instead of ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ [ap᾽ autou], from it. And in his Augustus an eagle-owl portended the war of Actium, flying into the temple of Concord, καὶ ἐπὶ τοὺς ἄλλους ἐπικαθήμενος [kai epi tous allous epikathēmenos], and perching on the others (that is, on the roofs of other buildings). Finally Ammianus, book 30, on the death of Valentinian: While he was still staying at Sabaria, an eagle-owl perched on the rooftops of the royal bath and hooted funereal notes, etc. We conclude, therefore, that the Psalmist's solitary bird, which keeps watch at night and perches on roofs, is not the sparrow, as they would have it, but the eagle-owl or the owl. The sparrow does indeed nest under the roof, but not על גג, upon the roof, as the Psalmist says.

VI. The sixth passage is Psal. CIV, 16: The trees of God shall be satisfied, the cedars of Lebanon, which he planted, where צפורים tsipporim make their nests. Trees of God, that is, very lofty trees. So also cedars of God, Psal. LXXX, 11; mountains of God, Psal. XXXVI, 7; flame of God, Cantic. VIII, 6, that is, a most vehement flame; wrestlings of God, Gen. XXX, 5, that is, most severe wrestlings. Thus trees of God and cedars of Lebanon are put forward as synonyms, since cedars are among the tallest of trees. And the trees of God and cedars of Lebanon are said to be satisfied, namely with rain, of which verse 13 speaks. And God is said to have planted them, like the aloe trees in Num. XXIV, 6, because they grow of their own accord, by God's will alone, without human labour and care. It is added that צפורים tsipporim nest in them, that is, sparrows, as many think. For so the LXX: Ἐκεῖ [II, 734] στρουθία ἐννοσσεύσουσι [Ekei strouthia ennosseusousi]. And Symmachus: Ὅπου στρουθία ἐννοσσεύσει [Hopou strouthia ennosseusei]. And the Vulgate translator: There the sparrows shall make their nests. And Apollinaris:
Κεῖσε νεηγενέων πέλεται στρουθῶν ἀλεωρὴ [Keise neēgeneōn peletai strouthōn aleōrē],

There is the refuge of newly hatched sparrows. And both Arabic versions: هناك عششت العصافير [hunāka ʿashshashat al-ʿaṣāfīr] There the sparrows nest. But Aquila, it seems, does better: Ἐκεῖ ὄρνεα νοσσεύσουσιν [Ekei ornea nosseusousin]. And Jerome: There the birds shall make their nests. For the summit of Lebanon, where the cedars are, is inaccessible to sparrows, which, as we have already shown, are not mountain birds.

VII. The seventh passage is Psal. CXXIV, 7: Our soul has escaped כצפור, like a tsippor, from the snare of the fowlers. The Greeks: ὡς στρυθίον [hōs strythion]; the Vulgate: like a sparrow; the Arabic likewise: مثل العصفور [mithl al-ʿuṣfūr] like the sparrow; Apollinaris: στρουθοῦ πανομοίϊος [strouthou panomoiios], entirely like a sparrow; but Jerome: as a bird. This I approve more, because sparrows and similar little birds are caught with birdlime rather than with a snare. This is taught by Baal Aruch on the word שפשף, which signifies a pole smeared with birdlime for catching little birds.

VIII. The eighth is Eccles. XII, 4 (var. 6), where the Greeks say of the old man: Καὶ ἀναστήσεται εἰς φωνὴν τοῦ στρουθίου [Kai anastēsetai eis phōnēn tou strouthiou], And he shall rise up at the voice of the sparrow. But Jerome: And he shall rise up at the voice of the bird. And the Chaldee: And you shall be roused from your sleep על עסק קול דעופא, because of the voice of the bird, that is, at the song of a bird, which some take to be the cock, and cockcrow to be meant. Just as the cock, which wakes people with its morning song, is simply called ales [the bird] in these lines of the Poet of the Amores, book 1, Eleg. 6:
And now Lucifer drives forth his frosty axles, and the bird rouses wretched men to their work.

Others prefer to understand the song of the sparrow or of a little bird, by which, however faint, the old man is woken from sleep, while the young sleep so deeply that they do not hear even the crash of thunder. Nor is it easy to decide which version is sounder. For we have amply refuted those who deny that the cock, or any of the larger birds, is signified by the word צפור. It can also be taken of the morning chatter of birds, which in Arabic is called by a most proper word, [col. 157] زقزقة [zaqzaqa] zakzaka. Alcamus: الزقزقة صوت طير عند الصبح [al-zaqzaqa ṣawt ṭayr ʿinda al-ṣubḥ] the chatter of birds about dawn.

IX. The ninth passage reads thus, Thren. III, 32: My enemies hunt me כצפור, like a tsippor, deservedly [sic]. Here the Greeks: ὡς στρουθίον [hōs strouthion]; but Jerome: like a bird. This I would rather take of the larger birds, on the catching of which effort is more willingly spent, and with greater profit.
